repos.title: Codebase-Memory: Tree-Sitter-Based Knowledge Graphs for LLM Code Exploration via MCP
repos.paper_summary:
Codebase-Memory is an open-source system that constructs a Tree-Sitter-based knowledge graph to expose structural code queries to LLM agents via the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The pipeline parses 66 languages, resolves calls using a six-strategy cascade, and detects communities with the Louvain algorithm. It stores the resulting graph in SQLite and exposes 14 typed query tools through a single statically linked C binary with zero runtime dependencies.

Evaluated across 31 real-world repositories, the MCP Agent achieved an 83% answer quality score compared to 92% for a file-exploration agent, while consuming ten times fewer tokens ($\sim$1,000 vs. $\sim$10,000) and requiring 2.1 times fewer tool calls. Query latency was under 1 ms for the MCP agent versus 10–30 s for the explorer. Limitations include reduced accuracy on macro-heavy C code (58% quality) and the absence of source-level context, which requires fallback to file exploration for exhaustive pattern matching.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Text-based code exploration by coding agents scales poorly, so the paper proposes a queryable code knowledge graph exposed via MCP.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work builds heavyweight code graphs or improves agent strategy, leaving the retrieval layer largely unchanged.

digest_headlines.heading: System Design
digest_headlines.headline: Codebase-Memory parses 66 languages into one SQLite knowledge graph and serves it through 14 MCP tools.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: On 31 languages the MCP agent scored 0.83 against 0.92 for the explorer while using 2.1 times fewer tool calls.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Structure helps cross-file queries, but results come from one backend and one repository per language.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion argues structural retrieval is a viable foundation for LLM-based code intelligence.

digest_headlines.heading: Data Availability Statement
digest_headlines.headline: The source code, benchmark scripts and evaluation data are public for the evaluated release v0.5.5.

repos.title: nanoMuse: An Open-Source Personal Agent for Every Device You Own
repos.paper_summary:
nanoMuse is an open-source personal agent that runs on a person’s own devices, including Android and desktop, to act on their accounts and files. It differs from Meta’s Muse by placing the agent directly on user hardware rather than in a cloud VM, providing direct screen control via "Hands," and using file-based memory readable by the user. Every action passes through a Sentinel policy gate that enforces scoped permissions and taint tracking for private data. The system supports multiple LLM providers and uses an optional relay server to sync conversations across devices.

The paper reports estimated resource costs: the Android app is 38 MB, while the desktop app ranges from 256 MB to 498 MB depending on the OS. A self-hosted relay requires approximately 85 MB of idle memory and costs USD 4–6 per month on minimal server tiers. Model usage costs are cited at CNY 2–12 per million tokens. Limitations include the lack of a privilege boundary separating the agent from credentials on a single device, the absence of reported success rates for screen operations, and the fact that memory entries do not yet track provenance or confidence levels.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: A personal agent should be inspectable by its owner, and no open counterpart to Muse existed before this report.

digest_headlines.heading: Personal Agents So Far
digest_headlines.headline: Before September 2026, open personal agents ran on the owner's machine without screens, and screen-operating agents served single tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: How Muse Is Built
digest_headlines.headline: Muse's shape rests on ten visible design choices and safety layers the agent cannot reach, with a virtual machine per person.

digest_headlines.heading: What a Personal Agent Should Be
digest_headlines.headline: A personal agent should answer five questions about memory, action, approval, learning and payment, across three horizons.

digest_headlines.heading: nanoMuse Today
digest_headlines.headline: nanoMuse runs one agent on each device, operating the Android phone's screen and the computer's, with a Sentinel gating every action.

digest_headlines.heading: A Roadmap With the Community
digest_headlines.headline: The open roadmap is set in three distances, from catching up with Muse to an open model for the hands and physical devices.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: nanoMuse's Sentinel shares a trust domain with the agent, and its hands have no measured success rate.

repos.title: The Other Half of the Memory Wall: Serving 35B MoEs from SSD with Trained Routing Prediction
repos.paper_summary: Edge0 is a streaming inference engine for 35B-class mixture-of-experts models on a 24 GB consumer machine. Expert weights stay on SSD and are memory-mapped on demand, so peak memory tracks the active experts, not all parameters. A per-layer prerouter head predicts the next layer's routing one token ahead, so expert reads overlap the current forward pass. The prediction is used as the routing itself, so the staged experts match the routed experts and none are dropped. An unmerged int4 recovery LoRA, distilled from the fp16 teacher on the student routing path, recovers quality lost to quantization and routing replacement. On a Mac mini M4 Pro with 24 GB, the 35B tier decodes at 20.4 tok/s with 2.9 GiB peak active memory, and the 8B tier at 28.0 tok/s with 1.5 GiB. On OpenCompass, the 35B tier averages 79.2 against 83.2 for its fp16 base, and the 8B tier 69.9 against 72.7. Limitations: AIME loses 6.1 points (35B) and 10.0 points (8B), requests are served one at a time, and CPU graph building sets a 44 ms per-step floor.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Storing 35B-class MoE weights on a 24 GB machine is the bottleneck, so Edge0 keeps experts on SSD and streams them.

digest_headlines.heading: Background and Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior offloading moves the weight footprint rather than shrinking it, and pre-gating schedules next-block experts too late for a streaming engine.

digest_headlines.heading: System Design
digest_headlines.headline: A 40-layer MoE needs 16.9 GiB of routed experts, so Edge0 mmaps them from SSD across four executor paths.

digest_headlines.heading: Training
digest_headlines.headline: Three training phases make the model work under replaced routing: head distillation, fine-tuning on the student path, and on-policy distillation.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Both tiers average within a few points of fp16 bases, and the prerouter adds +80 to +84% decode where weights do not fit.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Decode has a 44 ms per-step floor from graph building, quality loss concentrates in long-chain reasoning, and one backend exists.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: A 35B MoE runs at 20 tok/s in 3 GiB on a 24 GB desktop, with framework, checkpoints, and adapters open source.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix gives the softmax-top-k and sigmoid-group routing formulas and the incremental-stack assembly A/B results.

repos.title: DocLayNet: A Large Human-Annotated Dataset for Document-Layout Analysis
repos.paper_summary:
DocLayNet is a publicly available dataset of 80,863 human-annotated PDF pages designed for document layout analysis. The annotations consist of labeled bounding boxes across 11 classes (e.g., Text, Table, Formula) in COCO format. Unlike previous datasets derived from scientific repositories, DocLayNet includes diverse sources such as financial reports and manuals to capture layout variability. A subset of pages contains double or triple annotations to measure inter-annotator agreement.

Baseline experiments using Mask R-CNN, Faster R-CNN, and YOLOv5 show that model performance lags behind human annotation by approximately 10% in mAP@0.5–0.95. Specifically, the best-performing YOLOv5x6 achieves an overall mAP of 76.8%, compared to the human agreement range of 82–83%. A data ablation study indicates that model accuracy plateaus at 80% of the dataset size. Additionally, splitting data on document boundaries rather than individual pages reduces mAP by roughly 10 points, highlighting the risk of overestimation with page-wise splits. Models trained on DocLayNet demonstrate more consistent cross-dataset performance than those trained on PubLayNet or DocBank.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing layout datasets come from scientific repositories, so DocLayNet adds human-annotated pages with wider layout variety.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior layout analysis moved from rule-based methods to object detection, and newer text-plus-image models lack a shared data format.

digest_headlines.heading: The DocLayNet Dataset
digest_headlines.headline: DocLayNet contains 80863 pages from six document categories, with 11 labels and pre-defined splits that keep documents whole.

digest_headlines.heading: Annotation Campaign
digest_headlines.headline: Four-phase human annotation under a guideline over 100 pages long improved consistency, though 8 of 40 annotators did not pass.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Baseline detectors trail human agreement by 6 to 10%, and random page-wise splits inflate scores by about 10%.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: DocLayNet supplies human reference metrics and models that transfer better across datasets, yet a gap to humans remains.

repos.title: Democratizing Robot-Use Agents: A Unified Harness with Open Models
repos.paper_summary: uni-robot-agent is a unified, modular harness that lets open-weight models act as robot-use agents in simulation and on physical robots. It gives agents shared tools with common units and feedback across environments through per-environment adapters, overlaps model reasoning with tool execution, and binds images, calibration, and robot state to immutable snapshots. On RoboDojo's 42 simulation tasks (252 episodes), Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with the harness scores 31.39 with 25.00% success. This is above the published GPT-6 Astra–RoboProbe result of 28.97 and the listed VLA and WAM baselines, and the agent receives no simulator depth or task-verifier feedback. On 19 real-world tabletop tasks it scores 49.50, above Dream-1 (35.50) and close to a fine-tuned $\pi_{0.5}$ (47.75). Limitations: real-world agents receive RealSense depth while $\pi_{0.5}$ and Dream-1 use RGB only; precise manipulation and long-horizon execution remain weak, and Qwen and DeepSeek trail Xiaomi-Robotics-1 and OpenWAM-$\alpha$ on long-horizon tasks. Trajectory analysis finds four failure patterns, which the authors link to visual understanding, spatial grounding, geometric coding, and embodied reasoning.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Proprietary models block robot-use training, so this paper offers an open, trainable harness that reaches competitive scores.

digest_headlines.heading: uni-robot-agent: A Unified and Modular Harness
digest_headlines.headline: Shared tools, five logical layers, and six design choices let agents run without simulator depth or verifier feedback.

digest_headlines.heading: Can Open Models Use Robots in Simulation and the Real World?
digest_headlines.headline: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next reaches 31.39 Score on RoboDojo and 49.50 on 19 real-world tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: What Capabilities Enable Robot-Use Agents?
digest_headlines.headline: Robot use appears across model generations and families, and four failure types suggest joint training targets.

digest_headlines.heading: Analysis on Privileged Information
digest_headlines.headline: Removing camera parameters drops Qwen to 9.13, while removing skills changes Score from 31.39 to 30.31.

digest_headlines.heading: Analysis on Cost and Speed
digest_headlines.headline: Qwen costs 1.09 USD per episode for 31.39 Score, and pipelining cuts episode time on all five tested tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior robot-use harnesses offer varied tools and interfaces, so this work separates shared tools from model runtimes.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: An open-weight model with the harness reaches 31.39 Score, while precise manipulation and long-horizon execution remain open.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists baselines, real-world task catalogue and scoring rules, per-task results, and agent case studies.

repos.title: Memorilla: Latent Semantic Memory for LLMs
repos.paper_summary:
Memorilla is a memory system that gives a frozen LLM query-dependent access to a document collection by supplying a fixed number of soft memory tokens in its input embedding space. A frozen Qwen3-Embedding-4B encoder stores each document once, and a trainable module uses query-conditioned slots and Perceiver-style cross-attention over all stored embeddings to produce K=16 tokens for a frozen Qwen3-8B decoder. Training runs in three stages (Wikipedia paraphrase reconstruction, ten reading and QA datasets, then the eight evaluation benchmarks) using negative log-likelihood on answer tokens only.

Across eight benchmarks covering personalization, long-document QA and knowledge-intensive QA, the paper reports the best average performance among compared methods, including full context, RAG-50, MemoRAG, Mem0, xRAG and LLMLingua-2. On FactKG, accuracy is 84.33% versus 80.43% for full context, using 108× fewer document tokens. In TextWorld, RL training of the memory module raises success from 18.6% to 24.2% over full-history in-context learning.

Stated limitations: the encoder was not trained for compression, so fine-grained factual details can be lost, and experiments cover only one Qwen encoder-decoder pair and no coding domains.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Memorilla gives a frozen LLM 16 query-dependent memory tokens built from a whole document collection instead of retrieved text.

digest_headlines.heading: Memorilla
digest_headlines.headline: Documents are encoded once, and a trainable module maps each query to K=16 soft memory tokens for a frozen Qwen3-8B decoder.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Memorilla is compared with retrieval, compression and memory baselines on eight benchmarks using a frozen Qwen3-8B decoder.

digest_headlines.heading: Quantitative Results
digest_headlines.headline: Memorilla has the highest average score and leads on five of eight benchmarks, with a baseline ahead on NarrativeQA, PersonalizationV4 and PubMedQA.

digest_headlines.heading: What Does Memorilla Learn?
digest_headlines.headline: Memorilla's advantage over retrieval-augmented generation (RAG-50) grows with entity count, while retrieval wins on who and which questions in NarrativeQA.

digest_headlines.heading: Continual Learning with Memorilla
digest_headlines.headline: Reinforcement-trained memory on TextWorld raises the average solve rate and cuts rollouts that exhaust the token budget.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The learned memory interface can serve growing histories with a fixed token count, but it can lose fine-grained factual details.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists related work, training data and configuration, benchmark details, memory-token ablations and the TextWorld reinforcement-learning setup.

repos.title: OmniEdu: Open Foundation Models for Learning and Teaching
repos.paper_summary: OmniEdu is an open family of K–12 educational foundation models (4B, 9B, and 27B, fine-tuned from Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.8 bases) trained on a corpus organized around four capabilities: subject competence, curriculum grounding, diagnostic reasoning, and pedagogical action and scaffolding. A six-stage pipeline cleans and decontaminates sources, audits and rewrites examples with an LLM, scores quality on 1–5 rubrics, and performs token-budgeted diversity selection with k-center greedy over BGE-M3 embeddings. Each example then receives one of 20 task-specific pedagogical system instructions. The final mixture has 69,999 examples (60,951 education-specific) and 15.96M supervised response tokens. Models are trained with LlamaFactory for 3 epochs and compared with base models, open educational LLMs, and proprietary models. OmniEdu-27B reaches 63.12% EM and 76.69% F1 on K12-Bench (base 52.11% EM), 85.89% on MathFish, 86.95% MaC on EDUMATH, 78.74% Scaffold win rate on MathTutorBench, and a 3.02 Teaching average on LongTutor. Limitations: the paper reports that EDUMATH MaC trails Kimi-K3 (90.00%), and the pipeline depends on proprietary LLM auditors and scorers.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Educational models need problem solving, curriculum structure, diagnosis, and teaching, but these are often built and tested separately.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work spans open educational models, data-selection methods, and benchmarks, while many frontier tutoring systems remain closed.

digest_headlines.heading: Data Preparation
digest_headlines.headline: A six-stage pipeline cleans, audits, scores, and selects 60,951 education examples, then adds general data and pedagogical instructions for 69,999 examples.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Tuning improves each base model at all three scales across curriculum, problem-solving, and tutoring benchmarks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion argues capability-balanced supervision yields educational models that go beyond problem solving.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists per-subtask curriculum and general-capability tables and the full training configuration.

repos.title: OmniVoice: Towards Omnilingual Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech with Diffusion Language Models
repos.paper_summary:
OmniVoice is a zero-shot text-to-speech model covering over 600 languages. It is a single-stage non-autoregressive model: a bidirectional Transformer trained with a discrete masked diffusion objective maps text directly to 8-codebook acoustic tokens. Full-codebook random masking samples a mask for every token entry, so about 50% of tokens contribute to the loss, compared with one codebook per example in per-layer masking. The backbone is initialized from Qwen3-0.6B weights. The multilingual model trains on 581k hours from 50 open-source datasets.

On LibriSpeech-PC test-clean, it scores 0.729 SIM-o, 1.30 WER and 4.28 UTMOS, against 0.694, 1.59 and 4.28 for CosyVoice3. A bilingual variant trained on Emilia beats F5-TTS, ZipVoice and MaskGCT trained on the same corpus. Subjective SMOS is 3.80 versus 3.65 for Qwen3-TTS. On the 24-language MiniMax benchmark, Chinese character error rate is 1.008 versus 2.252 for MiniMax. Limitations: most baselines use different, larger training data; Cantonese word error rate is 17.709; and the FLEURS-102 results are not in the provided text.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing zero-shot speech models cover few languages, and two-stage discrete pipelines suffer error propagation and information bottlenecks.

digest_headlines.heading: Proposed Method
digest_headlines.headline: Full-codebook random masking and LLM initialization form the method, trained on more than 600 languages from 581k hours of audio.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Models are compared on Chinese, English and multilingual benchmarks using speaker similarity, error rates and subjective listening scores.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Results
digest_headlines.headline: OmniVoice gets the lowest word error rate on LibriSpeech-PC test-clean, at 1.30, and the highest subjective similarity score, at 3.80, among compared models.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude that the single-stage design, masking and LLM initialization together give broad language coverage and efficient inference.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists training datasets, inference-step and per-language results, supported languages, limitations and ethics statements.

repos.title: SUPRA-TEX: 3D Generation with Super-Aligned Texture
repos.paper_summary: SUPRA-Tex generates relightable 3D assets with PBR materials from a single reference image, keeping the reference's text, logos, and patterns at their visible surface locations. A 2D model built on a multimodal DiT predicts albedo and metallic-roughness maps in the reference view in one forward pass, taking 1.2 s on one H800. These maps are projected onto visible surface voxels and encoded by the frozen pretrained material VAE encoder into observation latents, which carry coverage and boundary-distance metadata. An interleaved flow transformer then generates full-surface material latents with flow matching. Observation latents serve as fixed, read-only memory, and blocks alternate between updating unobserved cells and the full surface. The 2D estimator is trained on Objaverse renders. The paper reports the best results among the evaluated methods in geometry-conditioned texturing and end-to-end generation, but the provided Table 1 excerpt cuts off before the SUPRA-Tex row, so this summary gives no SUPRA-Tex scores. Stated limitations include errors from upstream geometry or 2D material estimation, inconsistent completion across visibility boundaries, and qualitative-only failure cases with no paired two-view result.

digest_headlines.heading: 1 Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Multi-view fusion and native 3D generation both lose fine reference details, motivating a split into material estimation, alignment and completion.

digest_headlines.heading: 2 Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior texturing either fuses inconsistent multi-view predictions or conditions a native generator on implicit image features.

digest_headlines.heading: 3 Method
digest_headlines.headline: SUPRA-Tex estimates reference-view PBR maps, encodes them as fixed observation anchors, and completes the full-surface material latents.

digest_headlines.heading: 4 Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: SUPRA-Tex leads all shaded and PBR metrics in given-geometry texturing on both evaluation datasets.

digest_headlines.heading: 5 Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Errors in upstream geometry, 2D material estimates and unobserved regions limit fidelity and asset quality.

digest_headlines.heading: 6 Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Trained only on public data, SUPRA-Tex reaches top results among evaluated methods and is competitive with commercial systems.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix gives training data, optimization, evaluation protocols, ablations, extra qualitative comparisons and a notation table.

repos.title: Breaking the Space Barrier and its Application to Language Model Inference
repos.paper_summary:
*stcon* is a constrained-decoding engine for language models that applies constructions from a complexity-theory result on few-path graphs. The paper shows that deciding whether such a graph connects a source to a target is in ReachUL, LOGDCFL, C=L and SC2, using O(log²n / log log n) space, below Savitch's O(log²n) bound. For decoding, the token mask is recomputed on the GPU at each step instead of stored as a table, forced text is appended within the same model run, and independent JSON fields are decoded in parallel and verified against the model.

On one 16 GB Apple M2 Pro with Qwen3.5-2B and 4B (4-bit, greedy decoding), against MLX with llguidance, six JSON extractions finish in 1.89 s versus 2.41 s on the 2B and 3.89 s versus 4.59 s on the 4B. On the 2B, outputs match character for character. A 1,106-state tool-call grammar costs 3.4 MB instead of an 824 MB token table. Sixteen tool-calling agents finish in 29.3 s versus 74.6 s. Limitations: one machine and one model family, greedy decoding only, recursive grammars served one request at a time, and parallel decoding saves model runs but not wall time.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Constrained decoding adds per-step cost on a laptop, and this paper links it to a complexity question about few-path graphs.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: A laptop run is dominated by reading weights, and few-path graphs are defined as those with at most k walks between vertices.

digest_headlines.heading: The theory in plain words
digest_headlines.headline: Three ideas (budgets, certified fingerprints, one zero test) show total few-path reachability lies in ReachUL and related classes.

digest_headlines.heading: From the theory to the decoding engine
digest_headlines.headline: The decoding step graph is a tree, which yields six mechanisms for masks, forced text, budgets and parallel fields.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Six JSON extractions take 1.89 s on the 2B model against 2.41 s for MLX with llguidance, with the same answers.

digest_headlines.heading: Related work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work covers few-path complexity results and constrained-decoding libraries, and speculative decoding.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: The paper expects the gains on memory-bound devices, but tests cover one machine, one model family and greedy decoding.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The paper concludes that the same constructions settle few-path reachability and make structured decoding cheaper.

digest_headlines.heading: Statement of novelty
digest_headlines.headline: The author states the theory was obtained independently and the remaining time went to the practical engine.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers background, formal theory and proofs, the implementation, all measurements, negative results and tests.
